source.text: Καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ Ἰωάννου ὅτε ἀπέστειλαν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων ἱερεῖς καὶ Λευίτας ἵνα ἐρωτήσωσιν αὐτόν· Σὺ τίς εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: And this is the testimony of the John, when sent the Jews out of Jerusalem priests and Levites so that they might ask him, "You, who are you?"

en.L: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent out from Jerusalem priests and Levites in order that they might ask him, "You, who are you?"
en.B: This is what John testified when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?"
en.R: This is what John said when the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites, who served in the temple, to ask him, "Who are you?"

fr.L: Et c’est là le témoignage de Jean, quand les Juifs envoyèrent de Jérusalem des prêtres et des Lévites afin qu’ils lui demandent : « Toi, qui es-tu ? »
fr.B: Voici le témoignage que Jean rendit lorsque les chefs juifs envoyèrent de Jérusalem des prêtres et des Lévites lui demander : « Qui es-tu ? »
fr.R: Voici ce que Jean a dit quand les chefs juifs de Jérusalem lui ont envoyé des prêtres et des Lévites, qui servaient au temple, pour lui demander : « Qui es-tu ? »

sw.L: Na huu ndio ushuhuda wa Yohana, Wayahudi walipotuma kutoka Yerusalemu makuhani na Walawi ili wamwulize, "Wewe, u nani?"
sw.B: Huu ndio ushuhuda wa Yohana, viongozi wa Wayahudi walipomtumia makuhani na Walawi kutoka Yerusalemu ili wamwulize, "Wewe ni nani?"
sw.R: Hivi ndivyo Yohana alivyosema, viongozi wa Wayahudi huko Yerusalemu walipowatuma makuhani na Walawi, waliohudumu hekaluni, ili wamwulize, "Wewe ni nani?"

es.L: Y este es el testimonio de Juan, cuando los judíos enviaron desde Jerusalén sacerdotes y levitas para que le preguntaran: «Tú, ¿quién eres?».
es.B: Este es el testimonio que dio Juan cuando los dirigentes judíos enviaron desde Jerusalén a unos sacerdotes y levitas a preguntarle: «¿Quién eres tú?».
es.R: Esto es lo que dijo Juan cuando los dirigentes judíos de Jerusalén enviaron a unos sacerdotes y levitas, que servían en el templo, a preguntarle: «¿Quién eres tú?».

decisions.choice: the Jews: here the religious authorities in Jerusalem
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: John uses this word in several senses: the Jewish people (4:9, 22), people of Judea (11:19), and often the religious authorities in Jerusalem. Here they send priests and Levites from Jerusalem with official questions, and the envoys must report back to those who sent them (verse 22); verse 24 links the delegation with the Pharisees. That is the leadership, not the whole people. John the Baptist, Jesus and his first disciples are all Jews.

decisions.choice: priests and Levites: officials of the Jerusalem temple
decisions.reason: Priests offered the sacrifices in the temple. Levites, from the same tribe of Levi, assisted them and kept order there. Sending them makes this an official inquiry into who John claims to be.

decisions.choice: testimony: John's formal witness, picking up 1:7-8 and 1:15
decisions.reason: The opening said John came to testify about the light (1:7). What follows, up to 1:34, is that testimony: first what John says about himself (1:19-28), then what he says about Jesus (1:29-34). The word has the sense of evidence given before a court.
Σὺ stands first in the question. The envoys press John to say who he himself claims to be.

decisions.choice: the Jews (L); the Jewish leaders (B); the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: Literal shows the word John wrote; Balanced and Readable name the group the context shows (meaning decision m1), so no reader takes it as the whole Jewish people.
Readable says who the Levites were (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: narration in the passé simple (L, B), with Literal keeping John’s present tense ("il dit", "il voit"); passé composé (R); speech in the passé composé at every level
alternatives: passé composé for narration at every level
the present tense throughout at Literal
decisions.reason: The French brief for the whole passage (1:19-51). The passé simple ("envoyèrent", "répondit") is the normal tense of written narrative and suits a public reading; Literal uses it for the Greek past tenses and keeps the present where John tells a past event in the present (1:21 "il dit", 1:29 "il voit"), as the English Literal does. Readable uses the passé composé ("Jean a dit"), the past tense French readers speak and learn first. Inside speech every level uses the passé composé ("j’ai dit", "je suis venu"), as people speak. The imperfect ("baptisait", "connaissais") is used at every level for what was going on.

decisions.choice: les Juifs (L); les chefs juifs (B); les chefs juifs de Jérusalem (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John, first used here in this passage. Literal keeps the word John wrote. Balanced and Readable name the group the context shows (meaning decision m1): in French, "les Juifs" alone reads as the whole people. "Les chefs juifs" is plainer than "les autorités juives" and fits men who send envoys and expect a report; "les autorités juives" remains available where John means an official body.

decisions.choice: Wayahudi (L); viongozi wa Wayahudi (B); viongozi wa Wayahudi huko Yerusalemu (R)
decisions.reason: As the English and the book-wide choice for John: Literal keeps the word John wrote; Balanced and Readable name the authorities who sent the envoys, so the text does not set Jesus, John and his disciples, who were all Jews, against the Jewish people.

decisions.choice: los judíos (L); los dirigentes judíos (B); los dirigentes judíos de Jerusalén (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John, as in English: Literal shows the word John wrote; Balanced and Readable name the group the context shows (meaning decision m1), so no reader takes it as the whole Jewish people.
As in English: Readable says who the Levites were (meaning decision m2).
Standard Spanish typography, as in 1:15. Where a speech runs over several records, the guillemet opens in the first and closes in the last, as the English quotation marks do.

source.text: καὶ ὡμολόγησεν καὶ οὐκ ἠρνήσατο, καὶ ὡμολόγησεν ὅτι Ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ὁ χριστός.

records.literal_gloss: And he confessed and not denied, and confessed that "I not am the Christ."

en.L: And he declared openly, and did not deny [it], and declared openly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."
en.B: He spoke openly and did not refuse to answer; he stated plainly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."
en.R: John did not hide anything. He told them clearly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."

fr.L: Et il déclara ouvertement, et il ne [le] nia pas, et il déclara ouvertement : « Moi, je ne suis pas le {{christos:Christ|Messie}}. »
fr.B: Il parla ouvertement, sans se dérober ; il déclara clairement : « Ce n’est pas moi qui suis le {{christos:Christ|Messie}}. »
fr.R: Jean n’a rien caché. Il leur a dit clairement : « Je ne suis pas le {{christos:Christ|Messie}}. »

sw.L: Naye alikiri wala hakukana, na alikiri, "Mimi siye {{christos:Kristo|Masihi}}."
sw.B: Alieleza waziwazi, wala hakukwepa swali; alisema wazi, "Mimi siye {{christos:Kristo|Masihi}}."
sw.R: Yohana hakuficha kitu. Aliwaambia waziwazi, "Mimi siye {{christos:Kristo|Masihi}}."

es.L: Y declaró abiertamente, y no [lo] negó, y declaró abiertamente: «Yo no soy el {{christos:Cristo|Mesías}}».
es.B: Habló abiertamente y no se negó a responder; declaró con claridad: «Yo no soy el {{christos:Cristo|Mesías}}».
es.R: Juan no ocultó nada. Les dijo claramente: «Yo no soy el {{christos:Cristo|Mesías}}».

decisions.choice: declared openly, as one does in public or before a court
decisions.reason: ὁμολογέω means to say something openly or acknowledge it publicly; it is not admitting a sin here. Saying it, denying the opposite, and saying it again stresses how plainly John answered.

decisions.choice: did not deny: did not evade the question
alternatives: did not deny that he was the Christ
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. Placed between the two positive statements, it means John did not refuse to answer or hide behind vague words.

decisions.choice: emphatic I: I am not the Christ (someone else is)
decisions.reason: Ἐγὼ is emphatic. The envoys asked only who he was, but John answers the question behind it (compare Luke 3:15, where people wondered whether John was the Christ). The emphasis prepares for verses 26-27: he is not the one, but the one is already among them.

decisions.choice: the Christ: a title, the Anointed One, the king Israel was waiting for
decisions.reason: With the article, χριστός is a title here, not a name. 1:41 gives the Hebrew word, Messiah, which means the same.
Here the word is a title with the article, so every level writes "the" outside the span: "the Christ" or "the Messiah". The usual Balanced span would give "I am not Christ", which reads as a name.

decisions.choice: did not refuse to answer (B); did not hide anything (R)
decisions.reason: English "deny" needs an object; these say what meaning decision m2 finds.

A title with the article (meaning decision m4). French needs the article with either word ("le Christ", "le Messie"), so every level writes "le" outside the span; "Je ne suis pas Christ" would read as a name.

decisions.choice: Moi, je ne suis pas ... (L); Ce n’est pas moi qui suis ... (B)
alternatives: Je ne suis pas le Christ (L, B)
decisions.reason: The emphatic pronoun (meaning decision m3) is shown in French by a stressed "moi" (Literal) or by "c’est ... qui" (Balanced), which implies, as the Greek does, that someone else is. Readable keeps the plain statement.
French "nier" needs an object; Literal brackets it (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable follow the English wording.

Swahili has no article to mark "the Christ" as a title. "Mimi si Kristo" could be read as a name; "siye" (I am not the one) says that someone else is the expected king, as the meaning notes say. Both setting options read naturally with it.
As in English: here the word is a title with the article, so every level writes "el" outside the span. "Yo no soy Cristo" would read as a name.
Spanish "confesar" is heard first as confessing a sin, which meaning decision m1 rules out. "Declarar abiertamente" is saying something openly, as before a court.

decisions.choice: no se negó a responder (B); no ocultó nada (R)
decisions.reason: As in English: "negar" needs an object; these say what meaning decision m2 finds. Literal supplies "[lo]".

source.text: καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτόν· Τί οὖν;

records.literal_gloss: And they asked him, "What then?

en.L: And they asked him, "What then?
en.B: So they asked him, "Then what?
en.R: They asked him, "Then who are you?

fr.L: Et ils lui demandèrent : « Quoi donc ?
fr.B: Ils lui demandèrent alors : « Quoi donc ?
fr.R: Ils lui ont demandé : « Alors, qui es-tu ?

sw.L: Na wakamwuliza, "Basi nini?
sw.B: Basi wakamwuliza, "Ni nini basi?
sw.R: Wakamwuliza, "Basi wewe ni nani?

es.L: Y le preguntaron: «¿Qué, pues?
es.B: Así que le preguntaron: «Entonces, ¿qué?
es.R: Le preguntaron: «Entonces, ¿quién eres?

decisions.choice: What then?: if not the Christ, what are you?
decisions.reason: Τί οὖν is a short follow-up: if you are not the Christ, what is the answer? The exchange moves quickly, in short questions and shorter answers.
In English one asks "who" about a person; the sense is the same.
As in English: one asks "quién" about a person; the sense is the same.

source.text: σὺ Ἠλίας εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: You Elijah are?

en.L: Are you Elijah?"
en.B: Are you Elijah?"
en.R: Are you Elijah?"

fr.L: Es-tu Élie ? »
fr.B: Es-tu Élie ? »
fr.R: Es-tu Élie ? »

sw.L: Wewe u Eliya?"
sw.B: Je, wewe ni Eliya?"
sw.R: Je, wewe ni Eliya?"

es.L: ¿Eres tú Elías?».
es.B: ¿Eres tú Elías?».
es.R: ¿Eres tú Elías?».

decisions.reason: Malachi 4:5-6 (3:23-24 in the Hebrew numbering) says God will send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD. Elijah had been taken up alive (2 Kings 2:11), and he was expected to come back. John dressed as Elijah had (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6), so the question was a natural one.

source.text: καὶ λέγει· Οὐκ εἰμί.

records.literal_gloss: And he says, "Not I am."

en.L: And he says, "I am not."
en.B: He said, "I am not."
en.R: "No, I am not," he said.

fr.L: Et il dit : « Je ne [le] suis pas. »
fr.B: Il dit : « Je ne le suis pas. »
fr.R: « Non, je ne le suis pas », a-t-il dit.

sw.L: Naye anasema, "Mimi siye."
sw.B: Akasema, "Mimi siye."
sw.R: "Hapana, mimi siye," akasema.

es.L: Y dice: «No soy».
es.B: Él dijo: «No lo soy».
es.R: «No, no lo soy», dijo.

decisions.choice: John denies being Elijah himself come back
alternatives: John denies any link with Elijah
decisions.reason: Jesus says that John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12-13), and Luke 1:17 says John would go ahead of the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. John is not denying that role. He denies being Elijah himself returned, which is what he was asked; in this Gospel John always points away from himself to Jesus (3:30).

John often tells his story in the present tense ("he says", "he finds"), which makes it vivid. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English stories do. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: Je ne [le] suis pas (L); Je ne le suis pas (B, R)
decisions.reason: In a short answer French repeats the predicate with "le" ("Je ne le suis pas": I am not that one). The Greek has no such word, so Literal brackets it.

decisions.choice: historic present kept at Literal (anasema); past at Balanced and Readable (akasema)
decisions.reason: John tells past events in the present (he says). Literal keeps it, as the English Literal does; Balanced and Readable use the narrative past with -ka-, which is how written Swahili tells a story. This holds for the whole passage.
As in English: John often tells his story in the present tense. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as Spanish stories do. This applies throughout the passage.

source.text: Ὁ προφήτης εἶ σύ;

records.literal_gloss: The prophet are you?

en.L: "Are you the Prophet?"
en.B: "Are you the Prophet?"
en.R: "Are you the Prophet that Moses promised?"

fr.L: « Es-tu le Prophète ? »
fr.B: « Es-tu le Prophète ? »
fr.R: « Es-tu le Prophète que Moïse a annoncé ? »

sw.L: "Wewe ndiye yule Nabii?"
sw.B: "Wewe ndiye yule Nabii?"
sw.R: "Wewe ndiye yule Nabii aliyeahidiwa na Musa?"

es.L: «¿Eres tú el Profeta?».
es.B: «¿Eres tú el Profeta?».
es.R: «¿Eres tú el Profeta que Moisés prometió?».

decisions.choice: the Prophet: the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-18
alternatives: one of the old prophets come back
decisions.reason: The article points to a known figure. God told Moses he would raise up a prophet like him from among the people (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18). Later in John people wonder whether Jesus is "the Prophet" (6:14; 7:40), and Peter applies the promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22). Here, as in 7:40-41, the Prophet is treated as someone other than the Christ.
The capital shows a particular, expected figure (meaning decision m1), not any prophet.
Readable says which prophet is meant (meaning decision m1).
As in English: Readable says which prophet is meant (meaning decision m1). The capital shows a particular, expected figure.

source.text: καὶ ἀπεκρίθη· Οὔ.

records.literal_gloss: And he answered, "No."

en.L: And he answered, "No."
en.B: He answered, "No."
en.R: "No," he answered.

fr.L: Et il répondit : « Non. »
fr.B: Il répondit : « Non. »
fr.R: « Non », a-t-il répondu.

sw.L: Naye akajibu, "Hapana."
sw.B: Akajibu, "Hapana."
sw.R: "Hapana," akajibu.

es.L: Y respondió: «No».
es.B: Él respondió: «No».
es.R: «No», respondió.

decisions.reason: "I am not the Christ", then "I am not", and now a single word. The story shows John stepping out of the way.

source.text: εἶπαν οὖν αὐτῷ· Τίς εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: They said therefore to him, "Who are you?

en.L: So they said to him, "Who are you?
en.B: So they said to him, "Who are you, then?
en.R: So they said, "Who are you?

fr.L: Ils lui dirent donc : « Qui es-tu ?
fr.B: Ils lui dirent donc : « Qui es-tu, alors ?
fr.R: Alors ils lui ont dit : « Qui es-tu ?

sw.L: Basi wakamwambia, "Wewe u nani?
sw.B: Basi wakamwambia, "Wewe ni nani basi?
sw.R: Basi wakasema, "Wewe ni nani?

es.L: Le dijeron, pues: «¿Quién eres?
es.B: Así que le dijeron: «¿Quién eres, entonces?
es.R: Entonces le dijeron: «¿Quién eres?

decisions.choice: so: the question follows from his three denials
decisions.reason: οὖν links the question to what John has said: if he is none of these, who is he? It brings the envoys back to their first question (verse 19).

source.text: ἵνα ἀπόκρισιν δῶμεν τοῖς πέμψασιν ἡμᾶς· τί λέγεις περὶ σεαυτοῦ;

records.literal_gloss: So that an answer we may give to the [ones] having sent us; what do you say about yourself?"

en.L: [Tell us,] so that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
en.B: We have to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
en.R: We have to take an answer back to the leaders who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"

fr.L: [Dis-le-nous,] afin que nous donnions une réponse à ceux qui nous ont envoyés. Que dis-tu de toi-même ? »
fr.B: Il nous faut rapporter une réponse à ceux qui nous ont envoyés. Que dis-tu de toi-même ? »
fr.R: Nous devons rapporter une réponse aux chefs qui nous ont envoyés. Que dis-tu de toi-même ? »

sw.L: [Tuambie,] ili tuwape jibu wale waliotutuma. Unasema nini kuhusu wewe mwenyewe?"
sw.B: Tunapaswa kuwapelekea jibu wale waliotutuma. Unasema nini kuhusu wewe mwenyewe?"
sw.R: Tunapaswa kuwapelekea jibu viongozi waliotutuma. Unasema nini kuhusu wewe mwenyewe?"

es.L: [Dínoslo], para que demos una respuesta a los que nos enviaron. ¿Qué dices de ti mismo?».
es.B: Tenemos que dar una respuesta a los que nos enviaron. ¿Qué dices de ti mismo?».
es.R: Tenemos que llevar una respuesta a los dirigentes que nos enviaron. ¿Qué dices de ti mismo?».

decisions.choice: a purpose clause with its main verb unstated: [tell us] so that
decisions.reason: ἵνα begins a clause of purpose with nothing before it to depend on. The sense is "tell us, so that": the envoys must report back.

decisions.choice: those who sent us: the authorities of verse 19
decisions.reason: The envoys are not asking for themselves; they speak for the leaders in Jerusalem.
English cannot begin a sentence with "so that" alone (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: We have to give an answer ...
alternatives: so that we may give an answer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the purpose clause into a plain statement of need; Readable names the leaders (meaning decision m2).
As in English: the purpose clause has nothing to depend on (meaning decision m1). Spanish could begin with "Para que" alone in speech, but in writing it reads as a fragment.
As in English: Balanced and Readable turn the purpose clause into a plain statement of need; Readable names the leaders (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἔφη· Ἐγὼ φωνὴ βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ· Εὐθύνατε τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίου, καθὼς εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας ὁ προφήτης.

records.literal_gloss: He said, "I [am] a voice of [one] crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of Lord,' as said Isaiah the prophet."

en.L: He said, "I [am] a voice of [one] crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of [the] Lord,' as Isaiah the prophet said."
en.B: John answered in the words of the prophet Isaiah: "I am a voice of someone calling out in the wilderness, 'Make the road straight for the Lord.'"
en.R: John said, "I am the voice that the prophet Isaiah spoke about. Someone is shouting in the desert, 'Make a straight road for the Lord!'"

fr.L: Il dit : « Moi, [je suis] une voix de [quelqu’un] criant dans le désert : “Tracez droit le chemin du Seigneur”, comme l’a dit Isaïe le prophète. »
fr.B: Jean répondit par les paroles du prophète Isaïe : « Je suis la voix de quelqu’un qui crie dans le désert : “Tracez une route droite pour le Seigneur.” »
fr.R: Jean a dit : « Je suis la voix dont le prophète Isaïe a parlé. Quelqu’un crie dans le désert : “Faites pour le Seigneur un chemin tout droit !” »

sw.L: Alisema, "Mimi [ni] sauti ya [mtu] anayeita kwa nguvu nyikani, 'Nyoosheni njia ya Bwana,' kama Isaya nabii alivyosema."
sw.B: Yohana alijibu kwa maneno ya nabii Isaya: "Mimi ni sauti ya mtu anayeita nyikani, 'Mnyooshee Bwana njia.'"
sw.R: Yohana alisema, "Mimi ndiye sauti ambayo nabii Isaya aliizungumzia. Mtu anapiga kelele jangwani, 'Mtengenezeeni Bwana barabara iliyonyooka!'"

es.L: Dijo: «Yo [soy] voz de [uno que] clama en el desierto: “{{plural_you:Enderecen|Enderezad}} el camino del Señor”, como dijo Isaías el profeta».
es.B: Juan respondió con las palabras del profeta Isaías: «Yo soy la voz de alguien que clama en el desierto: “{{plural_you:Enderecen|Enderezad}} el camino para el Señor”».
es.R: Juan dijo: «Yo soy la voz de la que habló el profeta Isaías. Alguien grita en el desierto: “¡{{plural_you:Preparen|Preparad}} un camino recto para el Señor!”».

decisions.reason: Isaiah 40 opens God's message of comfort to his people in exile: the LORD himself is coming back to them, and a voice calls for a road to be made ready for him through the wilderness. John takes that voice as his own role. He is only a voice; what matters is the one who is coming. Isaiah's Greek has two verbs, "prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths"; John's words join them into one. Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3 and Luke 3:4 apply the same verse to John.

decisions.choice: Lord: in Isaiah 40:3 this stands for God's own name, the LORD
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 40:3 the word is the divine name. John prepares the way for Jesus, so the Gospel applies to Jesus a verse about the coming of the LORD himself (compare 1:1, 14).

decisions.choice: "as Isaiah the prophet said" is part of John's answer
decisions.reason: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the narrator introduces the quotation. Here the words continue John's reply: he himself names Isaiah as his source.

alternatives: as Isaiah the prophet said (at the end)
decisions.reason: After a quotation inside a quotation, a closing "as Isaiah the prophet said" is hard to follow in English. Balanced and Readable name Isaiah first; Literal keeps the Greek order.
The style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here the Gospel quotes the verse with the Greek word "Lord"; meaning decision m2 explains whom it means.
The word means empty country where few people live, such as the dry land along the lower Jordan. "Desert" is the everyday word for it.

Many French Bibles render the divine name of the Old Testament "l’Éternel". Here the Gospel quotes Isaiah 40:3 with the Greek word for "Lord", so French writes "le Seigneur"; meaning decision m2 says that in Isaiah the word stands for God's own name.

"Isaïe" is the form in general French usage and in Catholic and ecumenical Bibles; "Ésaïe" is the form of the Protestant tradition (the Segond family) and is common in Protestant churches, including in francophone Africa. A native reviewer should confirm which form the project uses; the choice must then hold for every book.

decisions.choice: Tracez droit le chemin (L); Tracez une route droite (B); Faites un chemin tout droit (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means "make straight". The familiar "aplanir" says "make level", a different picture; "tracer droit" keeps the straight line in ordinary French.

decisions.choice: « » for speech, “ ” for a quotation inside it
decisions.reason: Standard French typography: guillemets « » with a no-break space inside them, and English-style quotation marks “ ” for a quotation within a quotation, as here and in 1:30 and 1:33. A narrow no-break space goes before ; ! and ?, and a no-break space before a colon, so that no line begins with a punctuation mark.

In Isaiah 40:3 this stands for God's own name, which Swahili Old Testaments print as "BWANA". John quotes it with κυρίου, so the New Testament writes "Bwana", as the English writes "Lord"; the meaning note gives the Hebrew.
"Nyika" is open, empty country, the closer word; Readable says "jangwa" (desert), which young readers know better, as the English Readable says "desert".

decisions.choice: in water or with water: the water John immerses people in
decisions.reason: ἐν can name the element ("in water") or the means ("with water"); both describe the same act. The phrase is set against baptizing "in the Holy Spirit" in verse 33: John's washing is outward, and the one coming gives the Spirit.

decisions.choice: two statements side by side: I baptize; but among you stands one
decisions.reason: The second statement is John's real answer to "why do you baptize?": his baptism points to someone already present and not yet recognized (compare 1:10, the world did not know him). The perfect ἕστηκεν pictures him as having taken his place among them.

decisions.choice: the one coming after me: later in time, as in 1:15 and 1:30
decisions.reason: ὀπίσω can describe a disciple walking behind a teacher, but here, as in 1:15 and 1:30, it is the one who comes after John in time and ranks above him.

decisions.choice: untying sandals was a slave's task
decisions.reason: Sandals were tied on with leather straps. Untying and removing a master's sandals, and washing his feet, was the work of a slave (compare 13:4-14). John ranks himself below a slave beside the one who is coming.

decisions.choice: the Lamb of God: the lamb God provides as a sacrifice for sin; the Passover lamb and the lamb of Isaiah 53 are both in view
alternatives: a conquering leader, as the Lamb is pictured in Revelation
decisions.reason: Several Old Testament pictures meet here. In Genesis 22:8 Abraham tells Isaac that God will provide the lamb. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb protected Israel (Exodus 12); John later places Jesus's death on the day the Passover lambs were killed (19:14) and applies to him the rule that none of the lamb's bones may be broken (19:36; Exodus 12:46). Isaiah 53:7 compares the LORD's servant to a lamb led to the slaughter, and says he bore the sin of many (53:12). Lambs were also offered every morning and evening in the temple (Exodus 29:38-42). John does not choose between these, and the translation keeps the title as he gives it. A footnote gives the background.

decisions.choice: takes away: lifts sin up and carries it off

decisions.choice: sin, singular: the world's sin as a whole
decisions.reason: John speaks of the sin of the world as one great burden, not a list of wrongs.

decisions.choice: remained: the Spirit stayed on him, not just a passing visit
decisions.reason: μένω, "remain", is one of John's key words. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on prophets and leaders for a task; on Jesus the Spirit remains, and verse 33 makes this the sign God gave. Isaiah 11:2 says the Spirit of the LORD will rest on the king from David's line, and Isaiah 42:1 that God will put his Spirit on his chosen servant (compare verse 34). The same verb returns in verses 38-39.
The Greek perfect presents what John saw as standing evidence; English narrative uses the simple past. Literal keeps "I have seen".

The verb has no stated subject, and the word for Spirit is neuter in Greek, which says nothing about whether the Spirit is a person. English repeats "the Spirit" or joins the verbs, rather than calling the Spirit "it".
The pronoun refers to Jesus.

The French passé composé is both a perfect and a past tense, so every level keeps the Greek perfect without strain (unlike English, which needs "I have seen" at Literal and "I saw" elsewhere). Literal uses "contempler", the verb of looking with attention, as the same Greek verb is rendered in 1:14.

"Demeurer" is the word for the theological sense of this key verb (meaning decision m3) and keeps the link to 15:4; for young readers it is literary, so Readable says "rester", which carries the same sense. A reviewer may prefer "demeurer" at every level.

The Holy Spirit is a person, so "Roho" takes the personal agreement a-, as "Neno" does in 1:1. The subject of "remained" is then already in the verb, so Literal needs no bracketed "[the Spirit]". "Kukaa" is the word used for staying in verses 38-39 as well.

alternatives: the chosen Son of God (a few early translations)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts, including the oldest papyri that contain this verse, read "the Son of God". "The Chosen One of God" is found in the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and in some of the earliest Latin and Syriac translations; a few combine the two. The SBLGNT prints "Chosen One" as the harder reading: a scribe was more likely to change an unusual title to the familiar "Son of God", which John uses often (1:49; 20:31), than the reverse. The evidence is divided, so a footnote gives "the Son of God". Either way the title marks Jesus as the one God has set apart, shown by the Spirit. Reviewers should check this note against the apparatus.

en.R: They said, "Rabbi" (this means Teacher), "where are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} staying?"

fr.L: Et ils {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} dirent : « Rabbi » (ce qui, traduit, veut dire Maître), « où demeures-{{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} ? »
fr.B: Ils {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} dirent : « Rabbi » (ce mot signifie Maître), « où demeures-{{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} ? »
fr.R: Ils ont dit : « Rabbi » (cela veut dire Maître), « où loges-{{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} ? »

sw.L: Nao wakamwambia, "Rabi" (ambalo likitafsiriwa maana yake ni Mwalimu), "unakaa wapi?"
sw.B: Wakamjibu, "Rabi" (neno hili maana yake ni Mwalimu), "unakaa wapi?"
sw.R: Wakasema, "Rabi" (maana yake ni Mwalimu), "unakaa wapi?"

es.L: Ellos le dijeron: «Rabí (que traducido quiere decir Maestro), ¿dónde te quedas?».
es.B: Ellos le respondieron: «Rabí —que significa Maestro—, ¿dónde te quedas?».
es.R: Le dijeron: «Rabí (esto quiere decir Maestro), ¿dónde te estás quedando?».

decisions.choice: Rabbi: a respectful title for a teacher, which John translates
decisions.reason: Ῥαββί is a Hebrew title, literally "my great one", used for teachers of the law. John explains it for readers who do not know Hebrew or Aramaic, as he does with Messiah (verse 41) and Cephas (verse 42). By using it the two treat Jesus as their teacher.

decisions.choice: staying: where he is lodging, with the deeper sense of remaining in view
decisions.reason: μένεις is the ordinary "stay, lodge": they ask where he is staying so they can spend time with him. But it is the same verb as the Spirit "remaining" on Jesus (verses 32-33), and later Jesus calls his disciples to "remain in me" (15:4-10). John uses an everyday word that opens onto the deeper one; the wish to be where Jesus stays is where that begins.
The book-wide choice for John: the natural word in its ordinary sense, with the note giving the link to "remain".
The deity_pronoun setting covers every pronoun for Christ: "you" when people speak to him and "me" or "my" when he speaks of himself, as well as "he" and "him". "I" is capitalized either way.
Two Greek verbs ("is said", "being translated") make one English phrase.

"Où demeures-tu ?" is natural French for asking where someone is staying, and "demeurer" is the verb French uses for "remain" in 15:4-10 ("demeurez en moi"), so the link that meaning decision m2 points to stays visible at Literal and Balanced. Readable says "loger", the plain word for where one is staying; "habiter" would suggest a settled home, the sense m2 sets aside.
"Maître" is how French addresses a teacher with respect; "enseignant" and "professeur" name a job and are never used to address someone.

The French brief for the whole book: people say "tu" to Jesus, as to anyone they speak to alone, and he says "tu" to one person and "vous" to several. The deity_pronoun setting covers "tu", "toi", "te" when he is spoken to, and "lui", "le", "l’" when he is spoken of.

decisions.choice: unakaa: one verb for staying and remaining
decisions.reason: English has to say "staying" here and "remained" in verse 32. Swahili "kukaa" means both, so the link the meaning note points to (staying with Jesus, remaining in him) is kept at every level.

The ordinary word for where someone is lodging, as the book-wide choice asks. "Quedarse" is used for both verbs in verse 39, so the repetition of the Greek can still be seen; the meaning note gives the link to "permanecer".
Spanish addresses Jesus here with the verb and the clitic "te". The Spanish setting covers stressed pronouns only ("tú", "él", as in verse 49), following 1:1-18, so nothing is spanned here.
The traditional Spanish form of the title. "Rabino" now names a Jewish religious office, not a form of address.

fr.B: Il leur dit : « Venez, et vous verrez. »
fr.R: Il leur a dit : « Venez, et vous verrez. »

sw.L: Anawaambia, "Njooni, nanyi mtaona."
sw.B: Akawaambia, "Njooni, nanyi mtaona."
sw.R: Akawaambia, "Njooni mtaona."

es.B: Les dijo: «{{plural_you:Vengan y verán|Venid y veréis}}».
es.R: Les contestó: «{{plural_you:Vengan y lo verán|Venid y lo veréis}}».

decisions.reason: Jesus does not answer with an address. He invites them, and promises that they will see; the promise grows in verses 50-51, "you will see greater things". In John, seeing often leads on to understanding and believing.

alternatives: see (a command, in many later manuscripts)

Follows the SBLGNT future (meaning decision m2): Jesus invites them and promises that they will see.

source.text: ἦλθαν οὖν καὶ εἶδαν ποῦ μένει, καὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ ἔμειναν τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην· ὥρα ἦν ὡς δεκάτη.

records.literal_gloss: They came therefore and saw where he stays, and with him they stayed the day that; [the] hour was about tenth.

en.L: So they came and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they stayed with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} that day; [the] hour was about [the] tenth.
en.B: So they went and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they spent the rest of that day with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. It was about four in the afternoon.
en.R: So they went and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they stayed with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for the rest of that day. It was about four o'clock in the afternoon.

fr.L: Ils vinrent donc et virent où {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} demeurait, et ils demeurèrent auprès de {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} ce jour-là ; il était environ la dixième heure.
fr.B: Ils allèrent donc et virent où {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} demeurait, et ils demeurèrent auprès de {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} le reste de la journée. Il était environ seize heures.
fr.R: Ils y sont donc allés et ils ont vu où {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} logeait. Ils sont restés avec {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} le reste de la journée. Il était environ quatre heures de l’après-midi.

sw.L: Basi wakaja, wakaona mahali anapokaa, wakakaa pamoja naye siku ile; ilikuwa yapata saa kumi.
sw.B: Basi walikwenda, wakaona mahali alipokuwa akikaa, wakakaa pamoja naye siku ile iliyobaki. Ilikuwa yapata saa kumi jioni.
sw.R: Basi walikwenda, wakaona mahali alipokuwa akikaa, wakakaa pamoja naye kwa muda wote uliobaki wa siku ile. Ilikuwa kama saa kumi jioni.

es.L: Vinieron, pues, y vieron dónde se quedaba, y se quedaron con {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} aquel día; era como la hora décima.
es.B: Así que fueron, vieron dónde se quedaba y pasaron con {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} el resto del día. Eran como las cuatro de la tarde.
es.R: Así que fueron y vieron dónde se quedaba, y se quedaron con {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} el resto del día. Eran como las cuatro de la tarde.

decisions.choice: the tenth hour: about four in the afternoon
alternatives: about ten in the morning, counting the hours from midnight
decisions.reason: Jews and most people of the time counted the hours of daylight from sunrise, about six in the morning, so the tenth hour was about four in the afternoon; Jesus speaks of "twelve hours in the day" (11:9). Some have argued that John counts from midnight, as Roman documents sometimes did, which would make it ten in the morning. A footnote gives the literal wording and the other way of counting.

decisions.choice: stayed: the same verb as "staying" in verse 38
decisions.reason: μένει and ἔμειναν repeat the verb of verse 38: they see where he stays, and they stay with him. See the note on verse 38 for the deeper sense of "remain".

decisions.choice: that day: for the rest of the day, perhaps also the night
decisions.reason: The phrase says how long they stayed. Since it was already late afternoon, they spent the rest of the day with him, and perhaps the night.
The book-wide choice for John: clock times stay literal at Literal, and Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m1).
See meaning decision m3.
English tells the story from where the disciples were, so they "went".

decisions.choice: la dixième heure (L); seize heures (B); quatre heures de l’après-midi (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for clock times in John: Literal keeps the hour as counted from sunrise, Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m1, whose footnote gives the other way of counting). Balanced uses the twenty-four-hour clock of written French; Readable says it as people do aloud.

decisions.choice: demeurait ... demeurèrent (L, B); logeait ... sont restés (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 38. Literal and Balanced repeat one verb, as the Greek does (meaning decision m2); Readable uses the everyday words for lodging and staying.

decisions.choice: saa kumi at every level; jioni added at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: The Greek counts the hours from sunrise, and so does Swahili time. "Saa kumi" (the tenth hour) is therefore both the literal words and the right modern time, about four in the afternoon, and no level needs to convert it as the English does. Balanced and Readable add "jioni" (in the afternoon). "Saa nne" would be the international clock read in Swahili, which a Swahili reader takes as ten in the morning.

decisions.choice: como las cuatro de la tarde
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: clock times stay literal at Literal, and Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m1).
See meaning decision m3.
As in English: the story is told from where the disciples were.

source.text: ἦν Ἀνδρέας ὁ ἀδελφὸς Σίμωνος Πέτρου εἷς ἐκ τῶν δύο τῶν ἀκουσάντων παρὰ Ἰωάννου καὶ ἀκολουθησάντων αὐτῷ·

records.literal_gloss: Was Andrew the brother of Simon Peter one of the two of the [ones] having heard from John and having followed him;

en.L: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who heard from John and followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was one of the two who heard John's words and followed Jesus.
en.R: Andrew was one of the two who heard what John said and followed Jesus. Andrew was Simon Peter's brother.

fr.L: André, le frère de Simon Pierre, était l’un des deux qui avaient entendu Jean et qui {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}avaient suivi.
fr.B: André, le frère de Simon Pierre, était l’un des deux qui avaient entendu les paroles de Jean et suivi Jésus.
fr.R: André était l’un des deux qui avaient entendu ce que Jean disait et qui avaient suivi Jésus. André était le frère de Simon Pierre.

sw.L: Andrea, ndugu yake Simoni Petro, alikuwa mmoja wa wale wawili waliosikia kutoka kwa Yohana na kumfuata.
sw.B: Andrea, ndugu yake Simoni Petro, alikuwa mmoja wa wale wawili waliosikia maneno ya Yohana, wakamfuata Yesu.
sw.R: Andrea alikuwa mmoja wa wale wawili waliosikia Yohana alivyosema, wakamfuata Yesu. Andrea alikuwa ndugu yake Simoni Petro.

es.L: Andrés, el hermano de Simón Pedro, era uno de los dos que oyeron a Juan y lo siguieron.
es.B: Andrés, hermano de Simón Pedro, era uno de los dos que oyeron lo que dijo Juan y siguieron a Jesús.
es.R: Andrés era uno de los dos que oyeron lo que dijo Juan y siguieron a Jesús. Andrés era hermano de Simón Pedro.

decisions.reason: The two heard John and followed Jesus (verse 37).

decisions.choice: Simon Peter: the name readers know him by
decisions.reason: John calls him Simon Peter before Jesus gives him the name (verse 42), because his readers know him by it.

decisions.choice: the other of the two is not named
decisions.reason: John names Andrew but not the other disciple. Some have suggested it was the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is also never named (13:23), but this passage does not say.
See meaning decision m1.
See meaning decision m1. Literal keeps the pronoun, as the Greek does; it is the clitic "lo", which the Spanish setting does not cover.

source.text: εὑρίσκει οὗτος πρῶτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν τὸν ἴδιον Σίμωνα καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον χριστός.

records.literal_gloss: Finds this one first the brother the own Simon and says to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which is, being translated, Christ).

en.L: He first finds his own brother Simon and says to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which is translated {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}).
en.B: The first thing Andrew did was to find his brother Simon and tell him, "We have found the Messiah" (that is, the {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}).
en.R: Andrew first went to find his brother Simon. He told him, "We have found the Messiah!" (Messiah is a Hebrew word for the {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}, the king God promised.)

fr.L: Il trouve d’abord son propre frère Simon et lui dit : « Nous avons trouvé le Messie » (ce qui se traduit par {{christos:Christ|Oint}}).
fr.B: André alla d’abord trouver son frère Simon et lui dit : « Nous avons trouvé le Messie » (ce qui veut dire {{christos:Christ|Oint}}).
fr.R: André est d’abord allé trouver son frère Simon. Il lui a dit : « Nous avons trouvé le Messie ! » (Messie est un mot hébreu qui veut dire {{christos:Christ|Oint}} : c’est le roi que Dieu avait promis.)

sw.L: Huyu anampata kwanza ndugu yake mwenyewe Simoni, na kumwambia, "Tumempata Masihi" (ambalo likitafsiriwa ni {{christos:Kristo|Aliyetiwa Mafuta}}).
sw.B: Jambo la kwanza Andrea alilofanya ni kwenda kumpata ndugu yake Simoni na kumwambia, "Tumempata Masihi" (yaani {{christos:Kristo|Aliyetiwa Mafuta}}).
sw.R: Andrea alikwenda kwanza kumpata ndugu yake Simoni. Akamwambia, "Tumempata Masihi!" (Masihi ni neno la Kiebrania; maana yake ni {{christos:Kristo|Aliyetiwa Mafuta}}, mfalme aliyeahidiwa na Mungu.)

es.L: Este encuentra primero a su propio hermano Simón y le dice: «Hemos encontrado al Mesías» (que traducido es {{christos:Cristo|Ungido}}).
es.B: Lo primero que hizo Andrés fue buscar a su hermano Simón y decirle: «Hemos encontrado al Mesías» (es decir, el {{christos:Cristo|Ungido}}).
es.R: Andrés fue primero a buscar a su hermano Simón y le dijo: «¡Hemos encontrado al Mesías!» (Mesías es una palabra hebrea que significa el {{christos:Cristo|Ungido}}, el rey que Dios había prometido).

decisions.choice: Messiah: the Hebrew title, anointed one, which John translates
decisions.reason: Μεσσίαν is the Hebrew (and Aramaic) title written in Greek letters; John translates it with χριστός, the Greek word with the same meaning, "anointed". Kings (1 Samuel 16:13), priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil when God appointed them. By this time "the Anointed One" meant the king from David's line whom God had promised. Only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (here and 4:25).

decisions.choice: first (SBLGNT): the first thing he did
alternatives: he was the first to find (some manuscripts)
in the morning (a few early Latin manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have a form that makes Andrew the first of the two to find his brother; a few early Latin ones read "in the morning". The meaning changes only a little, so no footnote.

decisions.choice: We have found: the two disciples, and a discovery that holds
decisions.reason: "We" is Andrew and the other disciple. The perfect tense presents the finding as settled. Philip uses the same words in verse 45: each one who finds Jesus tells someone else.

decisions.choice: Messiah, plain; {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}} for the explanation
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for 1:41: Messiah is written plainly, since it is the word Andrew used. The christos setting is on the explanation only, and its alternative is "Anointed One", so no setting can produce "the Messiah (which means the Messiah)".
Balanced and Readable name Andrew for clarity.

decisions.choice: a Hebrew word for ... the king God promised
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the title meant (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: le Messie, plain; {{christos:Christ|Oint}} for the explanation, without an article
decisions.reason: As the English: "Messie" is the word Andrew used, so it has no setting, and the setting’s alternative is "Oint" so that no reader can get "le Messie (ce qui veut dire Messie)". The explanation names the word, so French needs no article, which also avoids a span that would have to switch between "le Christ" and the elided "l’Oint".

decisions.choice: Oint ... le roi que Dieu avait promis
decisions.reason: "Oint" is not an everyday word for young readers; as in the English Readable, the clause after it says what the title meant (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: Masihi, plain; {{christos:Kristo|Aliyetiwa Mafuta}} for the explanation
decisions.reason: As in the English: the Hebrew title is written plainly, and the explanation has its own alternative, so no setting can produce "Masihi (that is, Masihi)". "Aliyetiwa Mafuta" (the one anointed with oil) says what both titles mean.
The book-wide choice for 1:41: "Mesías" is written plainly, since it is the word Andrew used, and the setting is on the explanation only, so no setting can produce "el Mesías (es decir, el Mesías)".
Balanced and Readable name Andrew for clarity.

decisions.choice: una palabra hebrea que significa ... el rey que Dios había prometido
decisions.reason: As in English: Readable explains what the title meant (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἤγαγεν αὐτὸν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν.

records.literal_gloss: He led him to the Jesus.

en.L: He brought him to Jesus.
en.B: He brought Simon to Jesus.
en.R: Andrew brought Simon to Jesus.

fr.L: Il l’amena à Jésus.
fr.B: Il amena Simon à Jésus.
fr.R: André a amené Simon à Jésus.

sw.L: Akampeleka kwa Yesu.
sw.B: Akampeleka Simoni kwa Yesu.
sw.R: Andrea akampeleka Simoni kwa Yesu.

es.L: Lo llevó a Jesús.
es.B: Y llevó a Simón adonde estaba Jesús.
es.R: Andrés llevó a Simón a ver a Jesús.

decisions.reason: Andrew does not argue; he brings his brother. The pattern repeats through the chapter (verse 45) and later (4:29; 12:22).
Names make plain who brought whom.
Names make plain who brought whom.

source.text: ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Σὺ εἶ Σίμων ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωάννου, σὺ κληθήσῃ Κηφᾶς ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Πέτρος.

records.literal_gloss: Having looked at him the Jesus said, "You are Simon the son of John; you will be called Cephas" (which is translated Peter).

en.L: Jesus, looking at him, said, "You are Simon the son of John; you will be called Cephas" (which is translated Peter).
en.B: Jesus looked closely at him and said, "You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas" (which means Peter, that is, Rock).
en.R: Jesus looked straight at him and said, "You are Simon, son of John. But you will be called Cephas." (Cephas and Peter both mean Rock.)

fr.L: Jésus, fixant les yeux sur lui, dit : « Tu es Simon, le fils de Jean ; tu seras appelé Céphas » (ce qui se traduit par Pierre).
fr.B: Jésus le regarda attentivement et dit : « Tu es Simon, fils de Jean. Tu seras appelé Céphas » (ce qui se traduit par Pierre).
fr.R: Jésus l’a regardé droit dans les yeux et lui a dit : « Tu es Simon, fils de Jean. Mais on t’appellera Céphas. » (Céphas et Pierre veulent tous les deux dire « pierre » ou « rocher ».)

sw.L: Yesu, akimtazama, akasema, "Wewe ni Simoni mwana wa Yohana; utaitwa Kefa" (ambalo likitafsiriwa ni Petro).
sw.B: Yesu alimkazia macho, akasema, "Wewe ni Simoni, mwana wa Yohana. Utaitwa Kefa" (maana yake ni Petro, yaani Mwamba).
sw.R: Yesu alimtazama moja kwa moja, akasema, "Wewe ni Simoni, mwana wa Yohana. Lakini utaitwa Kefa." (Kefa na Petro yote mawili maana yake ni Mwamba.)

es.L: Fijando la mirada en él, Jesús dijo: «Tú eres Simón, el hijo de Juan; tú serás llamado Cefas» (que se traduce Pedro).
es.B: Jesús lo miró fijamente y le dijo: «Tú eres Simón, hijo de Juan. Te llamarás Cefas» (que significa Pedro, es decir, Piedra).
es.R: Jesús lo miró directamente y le dijo: «Tú eres Simón, hijo de Juan. Pero te llamarán Cefas» (Cefas y Pedro significan Piedra).

decisions.choice: Cephas and Peter both mean rock
decisions.reason: Κηφᾶς is the Aramaic word for rock, written in Greek letters; Πέτρος is the Greek word for a rock or stone, used as a name. John translates one by the other. Paul usually calls him Cephas (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9).

decisions.choice: you will be called: the new name looks ahead
decisions.reason: Jesus does not simply rename him; the future tense points to what Simon will become (compare Matthew 16:18). In Scripture God gives new names that mark a new calling, as with Abram and Jacob (Genesis 17:5; 32:28).

alternatives: son of Jonah, or Jonas (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read John here and in 21:15-17; many later ones read Jonah, as in Matthew 16:17 ("Bar-Jonah"). This John is not John the Baptist.
The same fixed look as in verse 36.

decisions.choice: that is, Rock (B); both mean Rock (R)
decisions.reason: "Peter" is a translation only for those who know Greek; Balanced and Readable give the meaning (meaning decision m1).
Readable marks the contrast between his old name and the new one.

decisions.choice: ce qui se traduit par Pierre (B); Céphas et Pierre veulent tous les deux dire « pierre » ou « rocher » (R)
alternatives: (ce qui veut dire Pierre, c’est-à-dire Roc), as the English Balanced
decisions.reason: In French, as in Greek, the name Pierre is also the common word "pierre", stone or rock, so the translation John gives already carries its meaning and Balanced needs no added gloss (meaning decision m1). Readable says it outright for young readers, adding "rocher" because a "pierre" can be small and the name points to something solid.

The passive future keeps the sense that the name is given to him (meaning decision m2); "tu t’appelleras" could be read as a plain statement of what his name will be. Readable says "on t’appellera", the everyday way to say the same.
Spanish readers may hear "piedra" in "Pedro", but it is still a name; Balanced and Readable give the meaning (meaning decision m1).
Readable marks the contrast between his old name and the new one.

source.text: Τῇ ἐπαύριον ἠθέλησεν ἐξελθεῖν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν.

records.literal_gloss: On the next day he wanted to go out into the Galilee.

en.L: On the next day [{{deity_pronoun:he|He}}] wanted to go out into Galilee.
en.B: The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee.
en.R: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee.

fr.L: Le lendemain, [{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}}] voulut partir pour la Galilée.
fr.B: Le lendemain, Jésus décida de partir pour la Galilée.
fr.R: Le lendemain, Jésus a décidé d’aller en Galilée.

sw.L: Kesho yake alitaka kwenda Galilaya.
sw.B: Kesho yake Yesu aliamua kwenda Galilaya.
sw.R: Kesho yake Yesu aliamua kwenda Galilaya.

es.L: Al día siguiente quiso salir hacia Galilea.
es.B: Al día siguiente, Jesús decidió partir hacia Galilea.
es.R: Al día siguiente, Jesús decidió ir a Galilea.

decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. The next sentence names Jesus as the one who calls Philip, and the story then moves north to Galilee (2:1).

John marks the days: the first day (1:19-28), the next day (1:29), the next day (1:35), the next day (here), and "on the third day" (2:1). Whether he means a week that echoes the week of creation, which his opening words recalled (1:1; Genesis 1:1), cannot be shown; at least the count ties the calling of the disciples to the first sign at Cana.
English needs a subject (meaning decision m1).
θέλω here is a decision to act, which he then carries out.

decisions.choice: alitaka, with the subject in the verb
decisions.reason: The English Literal brackets "[he]". Swahili carries the subject in the verb (a-litaka), so Literal needs no bracket; Balanced and Readable name Jesus, as the English does.
Spanish, like Greek, can leave the subject in the verb, so Literal needs no bracketed pronoun. Balanced and Readable name Jesus (meaning decision m1).
As in English: a decision to act, which he then carries out.

source.text: καὶ εὑρίσκει Φίλιππον καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀκολούθει μοι.

records.literal_gloss: And he finds Philip, and says to him the Jesus, "Follow me."

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} finds Philip, and Jesus says to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.B: He found Philip and said to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.R: He found Philip and told him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

fr.L: Et {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} trouve Philippe, et Jésus lui dit : « Suis-{{deity_pronoun:moi|Moi}}. »
fr.B: Il trouva Philippe et lui dit : « Suis-{{deity_pronoun:moi|Moi}}. »
fr.R: Il a trouvé Philippe et lui a dit : « Suis-{{deity_pronoun:moi|Moi}}. »

sw.L: Naye anampata Filipo, na Yesu anamwambia, "Nifuate."
sw.B: Akampata Filipo, akamwambia, "Nifuate."
sw.R: Akampata Filipo, akamwambia, "Nifuate."

es.L: Y encuentra a Felipe, y Jesús le dice: «Sígueme».
es.B: Encontró a Felipe y le dijo: «Sígueme».
es.R: Se encontró con Felipe y le dijo: «Sígueme».

decisions.choice: Follow me: the call to be a disciple
decisions.reason: The present command asks for continuing to follow. It is the same verb as in verse 37; here Jesus himself gives the call. The others in this chapter are brought by someone else.
As in verse 38: the setting covers every pronoun for Christ.
In Spanish the pronoun for Christ is a clitic joined to the verb; the Spanish setting covers stressed pronouns only, as in 1:1-18.

source.text: ἦν δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδά, ἐκ τῆς πόλεως Ἀνδρέου καὶ Πέτρου.

records.literal_gloss: Was now the Philip from Bethsaida, out of the city of Andrew and Peter.

en.L: Now Philip was from Bethsaida, from the town of Andrew and Peter.
en.B: Philip came from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter.
en.R: Philip was from the town of Bethsaida. Andrew and Peter came from there too.

fr.L: Or Philippe était de Bethsaïda, de la ville d’André et de Pierre.
fr.B: Philippe était originaire de Bethsaïda, la ville d’André et de Pierre.
fr.R: Philippe venait de la ville de Bethsaïda. André et Pierre venaient de là aussi.

sw.L: Basi Filipo alikuwa wa Bethsaida, kutoka mji wa Andrea na Petro.
sw.B: Filipo alikuwa mwenyeji wa Bethsaida, mji wa Andrea na Petro.
sw.R: Filipo alikuwa wa mji wa Bethsaida. Andrea na Petro nao walitoka huko.

es.L: Y Felipe era de Betsaida, de la ciudad de Andrés y de Pedro.
es.B: Felipe era de Betsaida, el pueblo de Andrés y de Pedro.
es.R: Felipe era del pueblo de Betsaida. Andrés y Pedro también eran de allí.

decisions.choice: city: a town of any size
decisions.reason: πόλις is any town with its own community. Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

decisions.choice: where they came from, not necessarily where they lived
decisions.reason: Mark 1:21, 29 places the house of Simon and Andrew in Capernaum, a few miles away. Bethsaida is the town they came from.
Bethsaida was a fishing town (meaning decision m1); in Spanish "ciudad" suggests a large place.

source.text: εὑρίσκει Φίλιππος τὸν Ναθαναὴλ καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Ὃν ἔγραψεν Μωϋσῆς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ καὶ οἱ προφῆται εὑρήκαμεν, Ἰησοῦν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρέτ.

records.literal_gloss: Finds Philip the Nathanael and says to him, "[The one] whom wrote Moses in the law and the prophets we have found, Jesus son of the Joseph, the [one] from Nazareth."

en.L: Philip finds Nathanael and says to him, "The one about whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets [also], we have found: Jesus, son of Joseph, the one from Nazareth."
en.B: Philip found Nathanael and told him, "Moses wrote about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the law, and so did the prophets, and now we have found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth."
en.R: Then Philip found Nathanael and told him, "Moses wrote about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the law, and the prophets did too. Now we have found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! His name is Jesus. He is the son of Joseph, from Nazareth."

fr.L: Philippe trouve Nathanaël et lui dit : « Celui dont Moïse a écrit dans la Loi, et les prophètes [aussi], nous {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}avons trouvé : Jésus, fils de Joseph, celui de Nazareth. »
fr.B: Philippe trouva Nathanaël et lui dit : « Moïse a écrit à {{deity_pronoun:son|Son}} sujet dans la Loi, et les prophètes aussi ; maintenant nous {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}avons trouvé : c’est Jésus, fils de Joseph, de Nazareth. »
fr.R: Ensuite, Philippe a trouvé Nathanaël et lui a dit : « Moïse a écrit sur {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} dans la Loi, et les prophètes aussi. Maintenant, nous {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}avons trouvé ! Il s’appelle Jésus. C’est le fils de Joseph, de Nazareth. »

sw.L: Filipo anampata Nathanaeli na kumwambia, "Yule ambaye Musa aliandika habari {{deity_pronoun:zake|Zake}} katika sheria, na manabii [pia], tumempata: Yesu, mwana wa Yusufu, wa Nazareti."
sw.B: Filipo alimpata Nathanaeli, akamwambia, "Musa aliandika habari {{deity_pronoun:zake|Zake}} katika sheria, na manabii pia waliandika, nasi sasa tumempata: Yesu mwana wa Yusufu, kutoka Nazareti."
sw.R: Kisha Filipo alimpata Nathanaeli, akamwambia, "Musa aliandika habari {{deity_pronoun:zake|Zake}} katika sheria, na manabii nao waliandika. Sasa tumempata! Jina {{deity_pronoun:lake|Lake}} ni Yesu. Yeye ni mwana wa Yusufu, kutoka Nazareti."

es.L: Felipe encuentra a Natanael y le dice: «Aquel de quien escribió Moisés en la ley, y [también] los profetas, lo hemos encontrado: Jesús, hijo de José, el de Nazaret».
es.B: Felipe encontró a Natanael y le dijo: «Moisés escribió acerca de {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} en la ley, y también los profetas, y ahora lo hemos encontrado: es Jesús, hijo de José, de Nazaret».
es.R: Entonces Felipe encontró a Natanael y le dijo: «Moisés escribió acerca de {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}} en la ley, y los profetas también. ¡Y ahora lo hemos encontrado! Se llama Jesús. Es hijo de José, de Nazaret».

decisions.choice: Moses in the law and the prophets: the Scriptures of Israel
decisions.reason: "Moses in the law and the prophets" names the Scriptures by two of their main parts (compare Luke 24:27, 44). Moses wrote of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18; see verse 21), and the prophets spoke of the coming king. Philip believes Jesus is the one they point to; Jesus says the same of the Scriptures in 5:39, 46.

decisions.choice: son of Joseph, from Nazareth: how people knew him
decisions.reason: This is how Jesus was ordinarily identified: by his father's name and his town (compare 6:42). John does not correct Philip. His readers already know from 1:1-14 where Jesus really comes from, and the question of his origin returns in 7:27-28 and 7:41-42.

decisions.choice: Moses wrote about him ... now we have found him
alternatives: We have found the one Moses wrote about ...
decisions.reason: The Greek puts the one Moses wrote about first and "we have found" late, building up to the name. Balanced and Readable keep that order by saying "him" twice.
The pronouns refer to Jesus.
French picks up "the one Moses wrote about" with an object pronoun before "avons trouvé", even at Literal, where it keeps the Greek order; the pronouns refer to Jesus and take the setting.

decisions.choice: Moisés escribió acerca de él ... ahora lo hemos encontrado
decisions.reason: As in English: Balanced and Readable keep the Greek build-up to the name by speaking of him twice.
The pronoun after "acerca de" refers to Jesus; the clitic "lo" takes no setting.

source.text: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Ἐκ Ναζαρὲτ δύναταί τι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι;

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Nathanael, "Out of Nazareth can something good be?"

en.L: And Nathanael said to him, "Out of Nazareth can anything good be?"
en.B: Nathanael answered, "Can anything good be from a place like Nazareth?"
en.R: Nathanael said, "Nazareth? Does anything good ever come from that town?"

fr.L: Et Nathanaël lui dit : « De Nazareth peut-il y avoir quelque chose de bon ? »
fr.B: Nathanaël lui répondit : « D’un endroit comme Nazareth, peut-il sortir quelque chose de bon ? »
fr.R: Nathanaël a dit : « Nazareth ? Est-ce que quelque chose de bon peut venir de ce village ? »

sw.L: Na Nathanaeli akamwambia, "Kutoka Nazareti kinaweza kuwako kitu chema?"
sw.B: Nathanaeli akajibu, "Je, kitu chema kinaweza kutoka mahali kama Nazareti?"
sw.R: Nathanaeli akasema, "Nazareti? Kuna kitu chochote kizuri kinachotoka katika mji ule?"

es.L: Y Natanael le dijo: «¿De Nazaret puede haber algo bueno?».
es.B: Natanael respondió: «¿Puede salir algo bueno de un lugar como Nazaret?».
es.R: Natanael dijo: «¿De Nazaret? ¿Acaso sale algo bueno de ese pueblo?».

decisions.reason: Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, never named in the Old Testament, and no one looked for the Messiah to come from it (compare 7:41-42, 52). Nathanael himself came from Cana (21:2), another town of Galilee.
The words alone do not show what answer is expected, but Nathanael's tone is doubtful: he cannot believe that anyone important could come from Nazareth.
Shows the doubt of meaning decision m2 in natural English.
Nazareth was a small village (meaning decision m1); French "village" says so plainly, where "ville" would make it sound larger.
Shows the doubt of meaning decision m2 in natural Spanish; Readable shows it with "acaso".

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Φίλιππος· Ἔρχου καὶ ἴδε.

records.literal_gloss: Says to him the Philip, "Come and see."

en.L: Philip says to him, "Come and see."
en.B: Philip said to him, "Come and see."
en.R: Philip answered, "Come and see for yourself."

fr.L: Philippe lui dit : « Viens et vois. »
fr.B: Philippe lui répondit : « Viens voir. »
fr.R: Philippe a répondu : « Viens voir par toi-même. »

sw.L: Filipo anamwambia, "Njoo uone."
sw.B: Filipo akamwambia, "Njoo uone."
sw.R: Filipo akajibu, "Njoo ujionee mwenyewe."

es.L: Felipe le dice: «Ven y ve».
es.B: Felipe le dijo: «Ven a ver».
es.R: Felipe le contestó: «Ven a verlo tú mismo».

decisions.choice: Come and see: the invitation Jesus gave
decisions.reason: Philip answers doubt the way Jesus answered the first two disciples (verse 39): not with an argument, but with an invitation to come and see.
The command is to see in person; Readable says so.
"Viens voir" is the natural French for this invitation; Literal keeps the two commands joined by "et", as the Greek has them.

decisions.choice: Ven y ve (L); Ven a ver (B); Ven a verlo tú mismo (R)
decisions.reason: "Ven y ve" keeps the two Greek commands, but "ve" is also the command "go"; Balanced uses the natural phrase. Readable adds "tú mismo", as English adds "for yourself".

source.text: εἶδεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν Ναθαναὴλ ἐρχόμενον πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ λέγει περὶ αὐτοῦ· Ἴδε ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν.

records.literal_gloss: Saw the Jesus the Nathanael coming toward him and says about him, "Look, truly an Israelite in whom deceit not is."

en.L: Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and says about him, "Look, truly an Israelite, in whom deceit is not!"
en.B: When Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said of him, "Here is a true Israelite: there is nothing deceitful in him."
en.R: Jesus saw Nathanael coming. He said, "Here comes a real Israelite! There is nothing false about him."

fr.L: Jésus vit Nathanaël venir vers {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} et dit de lui : « Voici vraiment un Israélite en qui il n’y a pas de ruse ! »
fr.B: Quand Jésus vit Nathanaël venir vers {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}}, {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dit de lui : « Voici un véritable Israélite : il n’y a aucune ruse en lui. »
fr.R: Jésus a vu Nathanaël arriver. Il a dit : « Voici un vrai Israélite ! Il n’y a rien de faux en lui. »

sw.L: Yesu alimwona Nathanaeli akija {{deity_pronoun:kwake|Kwake}}, naye anasema habari zake, "Tazama, hakika Mwisraeli, ambaye ndani yake hamna hila!"
sw.B: Yesu alipomwona Nathanaeli akija {{deity_pronoun:kwake|Kwake}}, alisema habari zake, "Huyu hapa ni Mwisraeli halisi, ambaye ndani yake hamna udanganyifu."
sw.R: Yesu alimwona Nathanaeli akija. Akasema, "Huyu anakuja Mwisraeli wa kweli! Hana uongo wowote."

es.L: Vio Jesús a Natanael que venía hacia {{deity_pronoun:él|Él}}, y dice de él: «¡He aquí verdaderamente un israelita en quien no hay engaño!».
es.B: Cuando Jesús vio que Natanael se le acercaba, dijo de él: «Este es un verdadero israelita: en él no hay engaño».
es.R: Jesús vio que Natanael se acercaba y dijo: «¡Aquí viene un verdadero israelita! No hay nada falso en él».

decisions.choice: an echo of Jacob, the man of deceit who was renamed Israel
decisions.reason: Isaac told Esau that Jacob had come "with deceit" and taken his blessing (Genesis 27:35), and the Greek translation of that verse uses this same word, δόλος. Later God renamed Jacob "Israel" (Genesis 32:28). Nathanael is an Israelite without the deceit of Jacob; verse 51 goes on to recall Jacob's dream. Psalm 32:2 blesses the one "in whose spirit there is no deceit".

decisions.choice: truly an Israelite: a true Israelite, worthy of the name
decisions.reason: ἀληθῶς qualifies "Israelite": Nathanael is what an Israelite should be (compare Romans 9:6).
δόλος is cunning or trickery. Nathanael's blunt question in verse 46 already showed that he says what he thinks.
Natural English for pointing someone out as he approaches.
These pronouns refer to Jesus; "him" in "said of him" is Nathanael and has no setting.

"Israélite" keeps the name Israel, given to Jacob, which the verse plays on (meaning decision m1); "Israélien" today means a citizen of the modern state, and "Juif" would lose the echo of Jacob. Readable keeps it too: the context makes it clear.
"Ruse" is the trickery Jacob used to take Esau’s blessing (meaning decisions m1 and m3), so the echo of Genesis 27:35 can be heard. Readable says "rien de faux", plainer for young readers.
Literal translates the adverb "truly" with "hakika" (surely, truly), because "kweli kweli" is kept for the double amen of verse 51 and the rest of John.

decisions.choice: he aquí (L); este es (B); aquí viene (R)
decisions.reason: Natural Spanish for pointing someone out as he approaches; Literal keeps "he aquí", as in verse 29.
Only the pronoun for Jesus takes the setting; "de él" and "en él" are Nathanael.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Πόθεν με γινώσκεις;

records.literal_gloss: Says to him Nathanael, "From where me do you know?"

en.L: Nathanael says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "From where do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"
en.B: Nathanael asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"
en.R: Nathanael asked, "How do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"

fr.L: Nathanaël {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} dit : « D’où me connais-{{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} ? »
fr.B: Nathanaël {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} demanda : « D’où me connais-{{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} ? »
fr.R: Nathanaël a demandé : « Comment est-ce que {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} me connais ? »

sw.L: Nathanaeli anamwambia, "Unanijua kutoka wapi?"
sw.B: Nathanaeli akamwuliza, "Unanijuaje?"
sw.R: Nathanaeli akauliza, "Unanijuaje?"

es.L: Natanael le dice: «¿De dónde me conoces?».
es.B: Natanael le preguntó: «¿Cómo es que me conoces?».
es.R: Natanael preguntó: «¿Cómo me conoces?».

decisions.choice: From where?: how is it that?
decisions.reason: Πόθεν literally asks "from where", and can also mean "how is it that" (as in Mark 12:37). The same word asks where Jesus himself is from (7:27; 9:29; 19:9).
See meaning decision m1.

decisions.choice: D’où me connais-tu ? (L, B); Comment est-ce que tu me connais ? (R)
alternatives: Comment me connais-tu ? at Balanced, as the English Balanced
decisions.reason: French "d’où" asks both "from where" and "how is it that", and "d’où me connais-tu ?" is the everyday question, so Balanced can keep the word that later asks where Jesus is from (7:27; 9:29; 19:9; meaning decision m1). Readable uses the plainest form.
"¿De dónde me conoces?" is natural Spanish, so Literal keeps the Greek word; Balanced and Readable say what it means here (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Πρὸ τοῦ σε Φίλιππον φωνῆσαι ὄντα ὑπὸ τὴν συκῆν εἶδόν σε.

records.literal_gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "Before the you Philip to call, being under the fig tree, I saw you."

en.L: Jesus answered and said to him, "Before Philip called you, being under the fig tree, I saw you."
en.B: Jesus answered, "I saw you while you were still under the fig tree, before Philip called you."
en.R: Jesus answered, "I saw you under the fig tree, even before Philip called you."

fr.L: Jésus répondit et lui dit : « Avant que Philippe t’appelle, quand tu étais sous le figuier, je t’ai vu. »
fr.B: Jésus lui répondit : « Je t’ai vu quand tu étais encore sous le figuier, avant que Philippe t’appelle. »
fr.R: Jésus a répondu : « Je t’ai vu sous le figuier, avant même que Philippe t’appelle. »

sw.L: Yesu akajibu, akamwambia, "Kabla Filipo hajakuita, ulipokuwa chini ya mtini, nilikuona."
sw.B: Yesu akajibu, "Nilikuona ulipokuwa bado chini ya mtini, kabla Filipo hajakuita."
sw.R: Yesu akajibu, "Nilikuona chini ya mtini, hata kabla Filipo hajakuita."

es.L: Respondió Jesús y le dijo: «Antes de que Felipe te llamara, estando tú debajo de la higuera, te vi».
es.B: Jesús le respondió: «Te vi cuando todavía estabas debajo de la higuera, antes de que Felipe te llamara».
es.R: Jesús le respondió: «Te vi debajo de la higuera, aun antes de que Felipe te llamara».

decisions.choice: being: Nathanael was the one under the fig tree
alternatives: Jesus was under the fig tree
decisions.reason: ὄντα agrees with "you": Nathanael was under the tree.

decisions.choice: Jesus knew what he could not have seen in an ordinary way
decisions.reason: Jesus saw Nathanael where no one could have told him, and Nathanael takes it as a sign of who Jesus is (verse 49). John notes elsewhere that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25; 4:17-18).

decisions.choice: the fig tree: an ordinary place of shade, with a picture of peace behind it
decisions.reason: John does not say what Nathanael was doing there. A fig tree gave shade near a house, and "each under his vine and under his fig tree" was a picture of peace in Israel (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). The translation leaves the image as it stands.

decisions.choice: I saw you ... before Philip called you
alternatives: Before Philip called you ... I saw you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable lead with the main statement; Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: Te vi ... antes de que Felipe te llamara
decisions.reason: As in English: Balanced and Readable lead with the main statement; Literal keeps the Greek order.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Ῥαββί, σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, σὺ βασιλεὺς εἶ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ.

records.literal_gloss: Answered him Nathanael, "Rabbi, you are the son of the God, you king are of the Israel."

en.L: Nathanael answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are King of Israel."
en.B: Nathanael answered, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are Israel's King!"
en.R: Nathanael answered, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God! You are the promised King of Israel!"

fr.L: Nathanaël {{deity_pronoun:lui|Lui}} répondit : « Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} es le Fils de Dieu, {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} es roi d’Israël. »
fr.B: Nathanaël répondit : « Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} es le Fils de Dieu ; {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} es le roi d’Israël ! »
fr.R: Nathanaël a répondu : « Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:tu|Tu}} es le Fils de Dieu ! Tu es le roi d’Israël, celui que Dieu avait promis ! »

sw.L: Nathanaeli akamjibu, "Rabi, {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} ni Mwana wa Mungu, {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} ni Mfalme wa Israeli."
sw.B: Nathanaeli akajibu, "Rabi, {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} ni Mwana wa Mungu; {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} ni Mfalme wa Israeli!"
sw.R: Nathanaeli akajibu, "Rabi, {{deity_pronoun:wewe|Wewe}} ni Mwana wa Mungu! Wewe ni Mfalme wa Israeli aliyeahidiwa!"

es.L: Natanael le respondió: «Rabí, {{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} eres el Hijo de Dios, {{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} eres Rey de Israel».
es.B: Natanael respondió: «Rabí, {{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} eres el Hijo de Dios; ¡{{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} eres el Rey de Israel!».
es.R: Natanael respondió: «¡Rabí, {{deity_pronoun:tú|Tú}} eres el Hijo de Dios! ¡Tú eres el Rey de Israel que Dios prometió!».

decisions.choice: Son of God: here a royal title for the Messiah, which the Gospel fills out
decisions.reason: Paired with "King of Israel", "Son of God" recalls God's promise to David's heir, "I will be his father, and he will be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14), and Psalm 2, where God calls his anointed king his son (Psalm 2:6-7). Nathanael means at least that Jesus is the promised king. John's readers already know that the Son is far more (1:14, 18), and the book is written so that they may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31).

decisions.choice: King of Israel: the promised king
decisions.reason: Zephaniah 3:15 calls the LORD himself the King of Israel in the midst of his people. The crowd greets Jesus with this title when he enters Jerusalem (12:13), and the notice on the cross calls him "King of the Jews" (19:19).

decisions.choice: King without the article: still definite
decisions.reason: The noun comes before the verb without the article, a common way to make such a predicate definite: Nathanael means the King, not one king among others.
As in verse 38. At the start of a sentence "You" is written plain.
Readable says what the title means here (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: roi d’Israël (L); le roi d’Israël (B, R), lowercase
decisions.reason: Literal follows the Greek, which has no article; French "tu es roi d’Israël" still reads as the one king (meaning decision m3). French writes titles such as "roi" in lowercase.
The stressed "tú" refers to Christ, so it takes the setting. At the start of a sentence "Tú" is written plain.
As in English: Readable says what the title means here (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: Amen, amen: a solemn pledge that what follows is true
decisions.reason: Ἀμὴν is a Hebrew word meaning "it is sure". People normally said it in response to someone else's prayer or oath (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus puts it before his own words, as a pledge of their truth. Only in John is it doubled, twenty-five times; this is the first.

decisions.choice: you: plural, addressed to more than Nathanael
decisions.reason: "He says to him" is singular, but ὑμῖν and ὄψεσθε are plural: the promise is for all the disciples.

Jacob dreamed of a stairway set on the earth and reaching to heaven, with the angels of God going up and coming down on it (Genesis 28:12); the words here follow the Greek of that verse closely. Jacob called the place the house of God and the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:17). Jesus says that he himself is where heaven and earth meet: the angels go up and down on the Son of Man. Together with the echo of Jacob in verse 47, the promise is that Nathanael will see more than Jacob saw.

The perfect participle says heaven has been opened and stays open: the way between God and people is open, as when heaven opened in the visions of the prophets (Ezekiel 1:1) and at Jesus's baptism (Mark 1:10).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus's name for himself, recalling Daniel 7:13-14
alternatives: a son of man: simply a human being
decisions.reason: In Hebrew "son of man" can mean simply a human being (Psalm 8:5; Ezekiel 2:1). In Daniel 7:13-14 one "like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule from God. In the Gospels Jesus uses the title of himself, and others only repeat it (12:34). In John the Son of Man has come down from heaven and will be lifted up (3:13-14). Nathanael has called him Son of God and King; Jesus answers with the title he chooses for himself.

decisions.choice: nawaambia, mtaona: the plural is in the verb
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to Nathanael but says "you" in the plural. Swahili marks the plural in the verb (-wa-, m-), so Literal needs no bracket; Balanced adds "nyote" and Readable "ninyi nyote" (all of you), as the English does.

decisions.choice: Mwana wa Adamu (for the whole book)
decisions.reason: The settled Swahili title; "Adamu" is also a word for humankind (as in "binadamu"), so it keeps the sense of "son of man" in Daniel 7:13. "Mwana wa Mtu" is more literal but unfamiliar. Never under the gender setting. For review by a native speaker.
